Covenant Radar Field Guide

How a credit desk uses Covenant Radar to see a covenant breach coming, decide what to do about it, and prove afterwards exactly why it acted. Every screen below was captured from the running application.

Environment

127.0.0.1:8000

Borrowers in scope

24

Exposure in view

₹4,270.52 cr

Personas

8 roles

Latest run

03 Sep 2026

Orientation

What the product does

Covenant Radar watches a portfolio of corporate loans and predicts which borrowers are about to breach a financial covenant — early enough to do something about it.

A covenant is a promise in a loan agreement: keep leverage under 3.00×, keep interest cover above 1.50×, keep the current ratio above 1.20×. Banks test these quarterly, after the borrower files financials. By then a breach has already happened.

Covenant Radar changes the timing. It combines each borrower's filed financial history with seven families of behavioural and external signals, projects each covenant ratio forward across 30/60/90-day horizons, and ranks the whole portfolio by how urgently it needs attention. A relationship manager opens the queue and works down it.

The product's defining commitment is evidentiary rather than predictive. Every figure on every screen is traceable to a stored record; the AI never calculates anything; every configuration change is version-controlled and approval-gated; and the entire decision can be reconstructed months later from a hash-chained audit trail. Most of this guide is really about that commitment, because it is what shapes the screens.

The three bands

Everything in the workspace resolves to one of three bands, set by threshold T1 against the escalation probability at the borrower's worst covenant and horizon:

BandProbabilityWhat it means for the deskSLA
Act now≥ 0.70Top of queue, a case is raised, a memo is offered24 h
Amber≥ 0.40Watched actively, case optional72 h
Watch< 0.40Listed, but not escalated168 h

A boundary value belongs to the higher band. And where confidence falls below the T2 floor of 0.50, no probability is shown at all — the screen says "Insufficient evidence — watching" and gives the reason instead. That rule holds across the API as well as the UI, so a bare number can never escape into a downstream system without its confidence.

Orientation

Signing in

Nothing renders anonymously. Every route redirects to /sign-in until a session exists.

The demo database seeds one account per role, all sharing the password CovenantRadar#2026. Signing in as each in turn is the fastest way to see how much the product changes shape by role.

UsernameRoleThe job in one line
rmRelationship ManagerWorks the queue; owns the borrower relationship
creditCredit OfficerRegisters covenants from documents; runs intake
approverCredit ApproverSecond pair of eyes on covenant registrations
riskRisk OfficerProposes thresholds; overrides risk views with reasons
riskheadRisk HeadApproves thresholds and model promotions
auditorAuditor / InspectorReconstructs decisions; exports evidence bundles
adminAdministratorUsers, access, jobs, configuration, retention
stewardData StewardImports statements; resolves quarantined rows

Rate limit

POST /sign-in is throttled per client. Switching personas rapidly — say, scripting all eight in a loop — trips it, and because the GET is throttled too the page comes back without a CSRF token. It looks like a broken login form, not a throttle. It clears on its own in 60–90 seconds; leave a couple of seconds between persona switches and it never fires.

Who can do what

Thirty-three permissions across eight roles. Navigation, buttons and routes are all gated from the same list, so a persona never sees a control it would be refused on.

Eleven permissions are held by everyone — the VIEW_* family covering queue, borrower, case, memo, covenant, forecast, evidence and document. Those are what make the workspace navigable at all. The table below shows only the permissions that differ, which is where the roles actually separate.

Two separations are worth calling out because they are the product's governance spine. The Credit Officer can register a covenant but not approve one — that needs the Approver, the Risk Head or an Administrator, and the maker-checker service refuses to let the same person do both. The Risk Officer can propose a threshold change but not approve it — only the Risk Head can. And the Auditor can read everything but change nothing: no memo generation, no simulation, no case updates. It is the only role with VIEW_AUDIT that cannot also act on what it sees.

Orientation

The workspace shell

One frame surrounds every screen: a permission-filtered sidebar in three groups, and a top bar carrying search, live activity, theme and the user menu.

The sidebar groups navigation as Monitor (queue, cases, notifications, search), Portfolio data (borrowers, facilities, portfolios, covenants, certificates) and Workflows (intake, financial statements, document review, simulator, audit, governance). An Administration group appears only for holders of MANAGE_USERS, MANAGE_JOBS or PROPOSE_THRESHOLDS.

Each link is individually gated, so the sidebar is the fastest read on what a role is for. Set the four side by side:

The top bar

Workspace search sits centre (press / to focus it). To the right: a Live activity toggle, a theme switch and the user menu.

Orientation

The seven stages

Every prediction is produced by the same seven-stage pipeline, and every stage is separately recorded. This sequence is the backbone of the explainability panel and the audit reconstruction alike.

Stage 1

Intake

Covenant terms extracted from sanction letters and amendments

Stage 2

Covenant Engine

Ratios tested against thresholds, per period

Stage 3

Evidence Ledger

Signals scored for persistence, materiality and decay

Stage 4

Forecast

Breach probability and crossing date per horizon

Stage 5

Intervention

Catalogue actions simulated against the forecast

Stage 6

Triage

Ranking, banding and case creation

Stage 7

Memo

Grounded narrative drafted from stored facts

The division of labour matters. Stages 1–6 are deterministic code. The model registry records the forecaster as deterministic / covenant-radar-deterministic-v1, and the explainability panel labels stage 4's decider as CODE. Only stage 7 uses a language model, and only to turn already-computed numbers into a sentence.

Persona 1

Relationship Manager

rm · relationship_manager

Works the portfolio queue top-down, opens case files, runs what-if simulations and logs the actions taken. Cannot upload documents, register covenants or ingest statements — this role consumes the analysis rather than producing the inputs.

13permissions

The portfolio queue

The landing screen and the product's centre of gravity. Twenty-four borrowers ranked by urgency — escalation probability multiplied by exposure and confidence — so row 1 is genuinely the borrower to open first.

Four filters narrow the list: band, SMA band (the Special Mention Account classification carried from account conduct, independent of the covenant forecast), case state, and signal family. The result count and a Save this view control sit directly above the table.

Expanding a row gives a triage summary without leaving the queue.

Why this score

The Why this score link opens the explainability panel — the answer to the question a credit committee will ask first.

The borrower case file

The case file is where a decision actually gets made. A header of borrower facts, a row of case actions, the AI explanation panel, and six tabs.

Tab 1 · Forecast trajectory

Tab 2 · Covenant position

Tab 3 · Financials

The most quietly rigorous panel in the case file, and worth understanding precisely because of the line it draws.

Below each chart is a "what moved it" sentence that does the analyst's first paragraph for them: "2.53× at FY24Q3 to 1.62× at FY26Q2. EBIT fell ₹9.10 cr (−36.0%) to ₹16.21 cr while finance cost held at ₹10.00 cr. The movement is entirely on the EBIT side." That decomposition into numerator and denominator is what turns a falling line into a cause.

Three further indicators — Debt/EBITDA, DSCR and EBITDA margin — appear in visually distinct dashed cards labelled "not covenanted". They are computed, not read, and the separation is deliberate: nothing on this panel should let a reader mistake an indicative ratio for a contractual test.

Tab 4 · Seven signal families

Tab 5 · Evidence

Tab 6 · Source documents

The intervention simulator

Having seen the problem, the manager asks what would fix it. The simulator answers with a comparison against doing nothing.

The comparison is the point. Against a baseline of doing nothing — 90-day probability 99.00%, crossing 28 Nov 2026 — CREDIT-REDUCE-DEBT-SERVICE returns a 90-day probability of 31.41% and no projected crossing within 90 days: a probability delta of −67.59%. Every column names its assumptions alongside its numbers, so the result can never be quoted without them.

Simulations are persisted write-once and deduplicated on the forecast, intervention and parameters, so a memo can cite a simulation and the citation stays reproducible.

Cases

One detail worth noticing: mentions outside the case scope are stored but never notified. The note keeps its full text for the record; the notification respects the scope boundary.

Persona 2

Credit Officer

credit · credit

Turns loan documents into machine-testable covenants, and financial filings into tested periods. Everything the Relationship Manager reads exists because this role put it there. Can register a covenant, but cannot approve its own registration.

19permissions

Covenant intake

Intake offers two routes to the same destination: upload a source document for extraction, or type the clause in by hand. Both run the same six verifications before anything can be registered — the screen says so explicitly, which is the whole design.

Here is the flow run end to end. A DSCR clause was entered by hand: "The Borrower shall at all times maintain a Debt Service Coverage Ratio of not less than 1.25:1, tested quarterly … with a cure period of thirty (30) days."

Supplying the effective date and re-running turns every verdict green, and a Confirm covenant control appears, alongside a bulk Confirm passing proposals that includes only proposals with every verification passed.

Registering and amending covenants

Persona 3

Credit Approver

approver · credit_approver

The Credit Officer's set plus one decisive addition — APPROVE_COVENANT — and one subtraction: no INGEST_FINANCIAL_STATEMENTS. The checker in the maker-checker pair, deliberately kept out of the data-loading path.

19permissions

The approval queue lives at /covenants/approvals and lists pending covenant registrations, amendments, waivers and retirements for a checker to decide, with a reason recorded either way. The maker's own requests are filtered out, so a user holding both permissions is never shown a control they would be refused on.

This screen currently fails

In this build /covenants/approvals returns HTTP 422 for every role that holds APPROVE_COVENANT — confirmed on both approver and admin. It is not a permissions problem. See Limits & open defects for the cause.

Model registry and evaluation

The intervention catalogue

The retired row rewards a second look. CREDIT-REDUCE-EXPOSURE is marked Retired, replaced by two entries: CREDIT-REPAY-TERM-DEBT for leverage, and CREDIT-REDUCE-DEBT-SERVICE for coverage and liquidity. The reason is arithmetic. "Reduce the funded exposure" is one business action with two opposite signs — it lowers a leverage ratio but raises an interest-coverage or current ratio. A single catalogue row can only carry one sign, so it was correct for leverage and backwards for the two minimum-threshold classes. Splitting it into two codes is the honest encoding.

Note also that the old row was retired rather than corrected. Persisted simulations are write-once and hash their catalogue inputs, so editing an entry in place would break every simulation already recorded against it — and any memo citing one.

Overriding a risk view

Reachable only by direct URL

This control is served as an embeddable fragment at /why/{subject_type}/{subject_id}/override, and its own markup declares it belongs on two surfaces — the case file and the why panel. Neither currently includes it, so it renders unstyled and standalone, and there is no link to it from anywhere in the UI. The endpoints work; the entry point is missing.

Persona 5

Risk Head

riskhead · risk_head

The Risk Officer's authority plus the three approvals that matter: covenants, thresholds, and model promotions. The only non-administrator who can change what the system believes.

23permissions

The Risk Head sees the same governance screen as the Risk Officer, with approval controls added on the Approvals tab. In this environment that tab reads "No threshold proposal is awaiting a separate approver" — nothing is pending, so no approve control renders.

The maker-checker rule is enforced in the service layer, not just the UI: a request cannot be decided by the person who raised it, and a checker's own requests are filtered out of their queue entirely.

Model promotion is approval-gated but not screen-exposed

APPROVE_MODEL_PROMOTION is held by the Risk Head and the Administrator, and the registry correctly refuses to promote forecast.ml_challenger without it. But the governance web routes cover threshold proposal and approval only — the model registry panel is read-only, with no promotion control. Promotion is presently a back-office operation rather than a screen action.

Two governance flows were not exercised in preparing this guide, because both mutate live configuration in ways that would change how the demo portfolio bands: submitting a threshold proposal, and approving one. The forms and the approval path are documented above from the screens and the service code; the write itself was deliberately left un-run.

Persona 6

Auditor / Inspector

auditor · auditor

Reads everything, changes nothing. The only role besides the Administrator with VIEW_AUDIT and READ_PERSONAL_DATA — and, unlike the Administrator, with no ability to act on what it finds.

11permissions

The audit trail

Warning reconstruction

This is the screen the whole product is built to make possible: take any forecast and rebuild, from stored records alone, exactly how it was reached.

The eleven parts, in order: Source data, Formula inputs, Covenant version, Thresholds in force, Calculation, Trend, Forecast, Evidence in force, Drivers, Memo and model-call record, Overrides and Dispositions.

The detail is complete rather than summarised. Covenant version gives the exact contractual terms as they stood — threshold 1.50000000, direction min, quarterly, period-end basis, effective 2024-07-01, warning headroom 10%, cure 120 days. Thresholds in force reproduces the entire T1–T12 snapshot that governed the run. This is what makes a months-old decision defensible: not a log line saying a number was produced, but the whole configuration it was produced under.

Evidence bundles

Persona 7

Administrator

admin · administrator

Identity, access, scheduled work, configuration and retention. Holds 33 of the 33 permissions — including ASSUME_PERSONA, which no other role has.

33permissions

Users & access

Every section demands a reason for change, and the screen closes with "All identity changes are recorded with before and after state." One consequence is spelled out rather than left to be discovered: narrowing a user's reach also narrows saved views that point at a portfolio they have lost — and never widens another user's view.

Operations

The seven jobs are the pipeline made operational: nightly.ingest → test → score → rank → update_cases → dispatch, wrapped by nightly.pipeline on a 0 1 * * * schedule. Each can be triggered manually, and a running job cannot be triggered twice.

The same screen carries retention. The regulatory floor is eight years and the log floor 180 days; raw signals and forecasts are held 24 months, notifications 12, resolved quarantine 90 days. A purge preview reports how many rows each rule would make eligible and at what cutoff, before anything is deleted.

Configuration

The proposal flow here adds something the governance screen does not have: you must see the blast radius before you can propose.

Not submitted

The preview above is read-only and was run for this guide. The proposal itself was deliberately not submitted — it would enter the approval queue and, if approved, re-band the demo portfolio.

Persona 8

Data Steward

steward · data_steward

Owns data quality: imports statements, resolves rows the importer refused, restates corrected periods, and maintains borrower and facility master data. Notably has no UPDATE_CASE, GENERATE_MEMO or RUN_SIMULATION — this role feeds the analysis without participating in the credit decision.

13permissions

Importing financial statements

That sentence is the design. A bad row in a financial extract is not an error to log and move past — it is a fact the bank does not yet have, and it needs a person. The importer accepts what it can, quarantines what it cannot, and reconciles against a control total.

Import not run

An import was not executed for this guide. The screen deduplicates on the extract's content hash: once a file has been imported, re-uploading it replays the stored report instead of importing. Running the prepared FY26Q3 extract now would consume it, and the next live demonstration would replay rather than import. The screen and its behaviour are documented; the write was left for the presenter.

Master data

Why the /master-data suffix

/borrowers/{reference} is claimed by the case file, so the master-data view is served at an explicit alias rather than at the bare path. If you are looking for the borrower edit form and finding the case file, this is why.

Reference

Shared controls

A few controls appear across personas and are easy to miss.

Two more worth knowing: every screen exposing a decision carries a Why? link to the explainability panel for that subject — forecasts, contractual status, signals and evidence each have their own. And evidence export is available from the queue and the audit trail as well as from reconstruction, for any role holding EXPORT_EVIDENCE.

Reference

Limits & open defects

What this guide could not verify, and what is genuinely broken. Recorded here rather than smoothed over, so that a reader who hits one of these knows it is not their mistake.

Defects found

1 · The covenant approvals screen returns 422

/covenants/approvals fails for every holder of APPROVE_COVENANT — verified on approver and admin.

The cause is an ordering problem in the pending-approvals listing. It iterates every pending maker-checker request and looks each one's operation up in a callback registry before filtering by the operations this service actually handles. The covenant approval service is constructed with an empty registry and a settings object enabling only the four covenant operations, so the lookup raises a validation error — surfaced as HTTP 422 — on any pending request it does not recognise.

The demo database contains exactly such a row: a pending model_registration request for the ML challenger, created by the governance seed. It is unrelated to covenants and would have been filtered out one line later. Because the registry is empty, the screen in fact only works when nothing at all is pending. Swapping the enabled-operations filter ahead of the registry lookup would fix it.

2 · The override control has no entry point

The override component declares itself as belonging to the case file and the why panel, but is included by neither template. Its routes work and its form renders, so OVERRIDE_RISK_VIEW is exercisable only by navigating directly to /why/{subject_type}/{subject_id}/override, where it appears unstyled outside the workspace shell.

3 · Model promotion has no screen

APPROVE_MODEL_PROMOTION is granted to the Risk Head and Administrator and is enforced by the registry, but the governance routes implement threshold proposal and approval only. The model registry panel is read-only, so an approved promotion cannot be performed from the UI.

Not exercised

  • Statement import. Not run, to preserve the prepared FY26Q3 extract for a live demonstration — the screen deduplicates on content hash and would replay thereafter.
  • Threshold proposal and approval. The band-impact preview was run; the proposal was not submitted, as an approved change would re-band the demo portfolio.
  • Covenant confirmation. Intake verification was run end to end and correctly blocked by a cure-window rule. No covenant was actually registered.
  • Case state transitions, memo generation and disposition recording. The controls and their gating are documented from the screens; no case was mutated.
  • SSO, SMTP and webhooks. Reported as unconfigured by the capability matrix, so the OIDC and SAML sign-in paths could not be exercised.

Empty in this dataset

Four screens show empty states because the seeded data does not populate them, not because they are broken: compliance certificates (no open requests), document review (no low-confidence OCR pages), quarantine (all four seeded import batches reconciled cleanly), and threshold history and drift (no prior snapshots or drift observations recorded).
